newsitem.title: UKRAINE: Government no danger to Ukraine c.bank, experts say.
newsitem.headline: Government no danger to Ukraine c.bank, experts say.

text.p: Ukrainian government criticism of the central bank highlights the woes of a country which has gone months without a budget, but is little more than political posturing, Western economists said on Friday.
President Leonid Kuchma, Prime Minister Pavlo Lazarenko and Economy Minister Yuri Yekhanurov all attacked the National Bank of Ukraine (NBU) this week.
"They need somebody to blame for Ukraine's economic problems," said one banker.
"The guys from the government often misunderstand the role of the NBU," said a Western economic expert, who asked not to be named.
Kuchma summoned central bank chief Viktor Yushchenko to his office on Thursday and urged him to "coordinate matters" with the government.

Yekhanurov told reporters on Wednesday that the government would force the bank to work with it while on Tuesday, Lazarenko broadly hinted to parliament that the NBU should provide direct credits to the government.
Lazarenko could be urging the bank to issue direct credits as parliament was more than two months overdue with the 1997 budget, said the Western economist.

"There are budget arrears, and that creates pressure on the government," he said, adding that the government had often relied on direct credits, which pushed annual inflation higher than 10,000 percent in 1993.
The economist said the bank would be reluctant to issue direct credits as Ukraine had agreed to follow tight IMF targets in the hope of getting a new $2.5-$3 billion loan.
The Extended Fund Facility loan depends on the budget and a tax reform package to underpin it being passed.
"If they started printing money the damage would be disastrous," one banker said.
Yushchenko, re-appointed to a four-year term by a big majority in parliament last month, said after the Kuchma meeting that the bank was opposed to issuing direct credits.
Ukraine is working on a law to lay down the role of the central bank, whose chief must report to parliament.
The economist said Lazarenko, who criticised the bank for not imposing a currency corridor or band, could be trying to appease exporters hurt by the hryvnia's rise in recent weeks.
"The NBU has introduced an informal trading band, and it's not falling in line with exporters or lobbyists who are pressuring the government," he said.
The hryvnia on Friday slipped to 1.8300 to the dollar from 1.8285 on the Ukraine Interbank Currency Exchange.
